title: Central Executive Network
subtitle: Holding goals during emotionally demanding tasks
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating central executive network across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
tags: established cognitive role; mixed disorder specificity
searchTerms: established cognitive role; mixed disorder specificity
learningObjectives: Explain central executive network in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in central executive network.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to central executive network.

sections.explainSimply: Executive networks support working memory, planning and goal-directed control.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Trauma symptoms can consume working-memory capacity, especially during cue exposure or sleep deprivation.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Frontoparietal control interacts dynamically with salience and default-mode systems; deficits may reflect state, avoidance, depression or medication effects.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of central executive network as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need central executive network to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Poor performance is not proof of structural impairment.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use central executive network to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses central executive network to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Poor performance is not proof of structural impairment. Evidence classification: established cognitive role; mixed disorder specificity.
